aquae [correctly: aqua] et igni interdictus — “Someone denied water and fire,” meaning denied hospitality. A Roman formula of outlawry.
There is no evidence at all that Schmitt was unwelcome in Dr Schranz’s house in Siedlinghausen in 1947. It is possible, however, that some of the other guests treated him with reserve.

Visit from Paul Adams — Paul Adams (1894–1961), editor of the cultural supplement of the Centre Party newspaper Germania. From 1934 he worked in radio in Munich and belonged to the Siedlinghausen circle. Schmitt regarded him as one of his closest friends. See p. 125.
Knappe — Karl Knappe (1884–1978), sculptor and stained-glass artist in Munich, and a friend of Konrad Weiß.
Rikus — Josef Rikus (1923–1989), sculptor. In January 1946 he moved to Siedlinghausen to work with the sculptor Eugen Senge-Platten (1890–1972). From 1947 he continued his training under Karl Knappe.

Möllenbrock — Klemens Möllenbrock, Die religiöse Lyrik der Droste und die Theologie der Zeit. Versuch einer theologischen Gesamtinterpretation und theologiegeschichtlichen Einordnung des “Geistlichen Jahres”, Berlin 1935; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Münster 1934.
Westemeyer — Dietmar Westemeyer, Donoso Cortés. Staatsmann und Theologe. Eine Untersuchung seines Einsatzes der Theologie in die Politik, Münster 1940; Spanish translation published in 1957.
Joseph Westemeyer (1908–1997) took the religious name Dietmar when he entered the Franciscan order.
The published book was based on his 1940 Catholic-theology dissertation at Münster.
Veit — Otto Veit, Die Flucht vor der Freiheit. Versuch zur geschichtsphilosophischen Erhellung der Kulturkrise, Frankfurt am Main 1947.
Memories of Walther Rathenau — On Schmitt’s relationship with Rathenau, see his account in Schattenrisse, as well as Tb 1912–15, pp. 333–335, and Tb 1921–24, pp. 103–107, 116–119.
Goethe, “We live …” — Probably Schmitt’s paraphrase of Goethe’s maxim:
“We all live from the past, and we perish from the past.”
paradisiacal little chambers — A phrase used by the Catholic pastoral theologian Johann Michael Sailer (1751–1832), which Schmitt may have known through Eschweiler.

See Karl Eschweiler, Die katholische Theologie im Zeitalter des deutschen Idealismus. Die Bonner theologischen Qualifikationsschriften von 1921/22. Aus dem Nachlaß hrsg. und mit einer Einl. vers. von Thomas Marschler, Münster 2010, p. 163.
Coclicus — Adrien Petit Coclico (1499/1500–after September 1562), composer and music theorist.
Huber’s dissertation — Kurt Huber (1893–1943), musicologist and member of the White Rose resistance group.
Kurt Huber, Ivo de Vento (ca. 1540–1575), Lindenberg im Allgäu 1918; doctoral dissertation in philosophy, Munich 1918.
in my essay on the taboo — Not identified.
Kalijarvi — Thorsten V. Kalijarvi, “Die Neutralität Amerikas,” in Europäische Revue 11, 1935, p. 721.
Kalijarvi (1897–1980) was professor of political science at the University of New Hampshire in the United States.
Lewis — Wyndham Lewis, The Enemy. A Review of Art and Literature, London 1927 ff.; idem, Hitler und sein Werk in englischer Beleuchtung, Berlin 1932; idem, Time and Western Man, London 1927.
In the second edition of Die geistesgeschichtliche Lage des heutigen Parlamentarismus, Schmitt had already referred in 1926 to Wyndham Lewis, The Art of Being Ruled, London 1926: GL, p. 11, n. 1.
The text here is in shorthand. It probably reads:
“did not arouse the hostility that I aroused.”
Essay by Hennecke — Hans Hennecke, “Wyndham Lewis. Vision und Satire,” in Europäische Revue 14, 1938, pp. 205–214.
Rosenbaum — Eduard Rosenbaum (1887–1979), Schmitt’s fellow student and friend from Strasbourg. See Tb 1912–15, pp. 404–405.
On 25 November 1950 he wrote against Schmitt in the Rheinischer Merkur under the title “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.”
It is unclear whether he had already expressed criticism of Schmitt in 1947.
“I do not know that I did well, but I did honestly” (Grey) — The British Foreign Secretary Edward Grey (1862–1933) wrote this sentence to his wife in 1906.
See Viscount Grey of Fallodon, Twenty Five Years, vol. 1, Toronto 1923, p. 79.
Film — Schmitt’s attitude toward film here was completely different from his attitude in the 1920s and 1930s. Compare his diaries.
“All I inherited was my own body …” — Richard Wagner, Götterdämmerung, Act I, Scene 2.
Podszus — Friedrich Podszus (1899–1971), literary scholar and editor, and co-editor of the two-volume Benjamin edition of 1955.

See Helmut Peitsch, “Wolf von Niebelschütz, Walter Benjamin und ihre Leser im ‘Dritten Reich’. Zur Erinnerung an Friedrich Podszus,” in LiLi. Zeitschrift für Literaturwissenschaft und Linguistik 16, 1986, pp. 170–178.
Binaris numerus infamis — “Two is an evil number.” Meister Eckhart.
See Wouter Goris, Einheit als Prinzip und Ziel. Versuch über die Einheitsmetaphysik des Opus tripartitum Meister Eckharts, Leiden/New York/Cologne 1997, pp. 106 ff.

Drucker, “For Jews always remain Jews …” — Peter F. Drucker (1909–2005), Austrian economist. He emigrated to England in 1933 and became a US citizen in 1943. He later became an influential writer and teacher on management.
Peter F. Drucker, The End of Economic Man: The Origins of Totalitarianism, first edition, London 1943; German: Ursprung des Totalitarismus. Das Ende des Homo Oeconomicus, Vienna 2010.
In the third edition, New Brunswick/London 1995, reprinted 2009, the first sentence quoted by Schmitt appears on p. 213:
“To the extent that the problem of self-assertion and self-justification becomes more and more urgent, totalitarianism must invent new personifications of new demons.”
The second sentence appears on p. 209:
“In comparison with the Jews, even the Communists are of doubtful value as demonic enemies.”

“For Jews always remain Jews. A Communist, by contrast, can improve and change. This has nothing to do with Nordic race and so on. It is precisely the assimilated Jew who is the true enemy. There is no point at all in proving the Protocols of the Elders of Zion false.”
These five sentences summarize the following four passages from Drucker:
“For the individual Communist can always recant; but, once a Jew, always a Jew.” (p. 209)

“Nazi anti-Semitism is therefore due neither to the irreconcilable conflict between the Nordic and the Semitic principle as the Nazis assert, nor to the inherent anti-Semitism of the German People, as is so often said in the outside world.” (p. 209)
“The Nazis do not persecute the Jews because they remained a foreign body within Germany, but actually because they had become almost completely assimilated and had ceased to be Jews.” (pp. 209–210)
“The famous Protocols of Zion can be proved a hundred times a clumsy forgery; they must be genuine, as the Jewish conspiracy against Germany must be real.” (p. 210)
Bernanos — Georges Bernanos, La France contre les Robots, 40th ed., Paris 1947; German: Wider die Roboter, Cologne 1949.
ubi nihil vales ibi nihil velis — “Where you have no power, desire nothing.”
A phrase frequently quoted by the Flemish theologian and philosopher Arnold Geulincx (1624–1669).
Schmitt often used it as a formula of detachment, for example in relation to organized Catholicism. See Gespräch, p. 57.
Fritz Eisler — (1887–1914), Schmitt’s friend from his student years. Schmitt dedicated his 1916 book on Däubler and his 1928 Constitutional Theory to Eisler.
See Reinhard Mehring, Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 2), Plettenberg 2009.
“the living garment of the Godhead” — Goethe, Faust, Part I, “Study.”
Nebel — Gerhard Nebel (1903–1974), writer, whose difficult and contradictory relationship with Schmitt went back to 1933.
Nebel’s Platon und die Polis appeared in 1947. In a letter to Nebel dated 10 October 1947, Schmitt praised the study enthusiastically.
See Ernst Jünger / Gerhard Nebel, Briefe 1938–1974, ed. U. Fröschle and M. Neumann, Stuttgart 2003, p. 608.
Jaeger — Werner Jaeger, Paideia. Die Formung des griechischen Menschen, first ed., Berlin/Leipzig 1934.
πάντα [γάρ] τολμητέον — “For one must dare everything.”
“But what if we were to dare to be completely shameless?”
καλός [γάρ ὁ] κίνδυνος — “For the risk is beautiful.”

“… this, I think, is fitting and is worth risking: that one should believe things are so. For it is a beautiful risk, and one must as it were enchant oneself with such things. That is why I have been spinning out the story for so long. For this reason, a man should be of good courage concerning his soul …”
The immortality of the soul, although repeatedly “proved” in the Phaedo, nevertheless remains a myth—but a beautiful risk.

See Eveline Krummen, “‘Schön ist das Wagnis’. Rituelle Handlung und mythische Erzählung in Platons Phaidon,” in A. Bierl / R. Lämmle / K. Wesselmann (eds.), Literatur und Religion. Wege zu einer mythisch-rituellen Poetik bei den Griechen, vol. 2, Berlin/New York 2007, pp. 91–139.
ne simus faciles … — “Let us not be careless with words. Truth lies in the Word of God.”
See also C. Schmitt, Die Tyrannei der Werte, 3rd corrected ed., Berlin 2011, p. 52.
It reverses the Latin proverb In verbis simus faciles—“Let us be easygoing in words.”
Bismarck ended his Gedanken und Erinnerungen with that phrase, which Schmitt thought showed “a very high degree of head-forester mentality.”
See BW EJ, p. 175 and the commentary there, p. 605; see also below on p. 69.
Mme Guyon — Jeanne Marie Guyon du Chesnoy (1648–1717), mystic whose many writings strongly influenced, among other things, German Pietism.

Schmitt probably knew her through his study of Pietism. See Johann Arnold Kanne, Aus meinem Leben. Aufzeichnungen des deutschen Pietisten Johann Kanne, ed. Carl Schmitt-Dorotić, Berlin 1919; reprint Vienna 1994.
Schmitt quotes Guyon in his Political Romanticism: PR, p. 38, n. 1.
“The path of spirit is the detour” — “Nature reaches its goal by the shortest route. That is true; but the path of spirit is mediation, the detour.”
G. W. F. Hegel, Vorlesungen über die Geschichte der Philosophie, in Werke, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 18, Frankfurt am Main 1979, p. 55.
Donoso, “Seuls aujourd’hui …” — Schmitt quotes from the following edition: Juan Donoso Cortés, Oeuvres, vol. 2, Paris 1858, p. 165 (RW 265 no. 23878).

“For tyrants—in the form of emperors, kings, popes, Jesuits, generals, diplomats—have until now been able, at the decisive moment, to govern and direct the world. But from the time the Fourth Estate is established—once this fact has had enough time to become established in such a way that people truly understand it—it will become clear that only martyrs can govern the world at the decisive moment.”
S. Kierkegaard, Das Buch über Adler, Düsseldorf/Cologne 1962, p. 207.
Schmitt refers to this passage in C. Schmitt, Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation, Cologne 1950, p. 107.
